body_markdown:
It makes me smile to recall my first overseas press launch as a reporter for the trade tabloid *Automotive News* . On that first night in Stuttgart, a gaggle of jet-lagged journalists assembled for a briefing on the new Mercedes-Benz S-Class, the sleek and slippery W220. Benz passenger car chief Jürgen Hubbert entered the room with his entourage, strode up to one of our number, and instead of saying “hallo” or “welcome,” demanded, “Ver is your tie?” I was in the clear; my father taught me to dress at the expected level of the people I would be meeting, and in those days, it was understood that German auto execs would be in coats and ties.


I largely left the press-trip racket a while ago, but nowadays when I’m on the occasional launch, I marvel at the hoodies, sweatpants, and trucker caps that seem to be a permanent second skin for the influencer and vlogger horde that now constitutes much of automotive media. Casual has its place, but a hyper-casual, I-just-pulled-this-off-the-laundry-pile aesthetic seems to be all there is today, the only thing separating a Nordstrom from a Marshalls being the price of their flannel.


Mike Shaffer


Mike Shaffer


Recently, at a vintage racing event at the Goodwood Circuit in England, where people tend to dress up, I noticed that the public spaces were immaculate. Not a piece of trash in sight, though the many vendors served everything from sushi and sausage rolls on paper plates to Old Speckled Hen in plastic pint cups. It’s not a cultural thing; the Brits can be as messy and nasty in public as anyone. After declining for years, the number of football (soccer) matches with reported incidents of violence or rowdiness in the U.K. has risen the past two years, according to police stats. But the Goodwood Revival in September hosts close to 150,000 over three days and, though I’ve been many times, I’ve never heard a sharp word, much less witnessed a physical altercation. There’s barely any visible security.


James Lipman


Hagerty contributor Lyn Woodward has a theory I happen to agree with: The act of dressing up, whether at Goodwood or elsewhere, causes people to behave differently. Wearing your Sunday best makes you inclined to behave your Sunday best, in other words. One big reason we like old cars is that they are time machines, and the times they come from were largely more formal than today. Whether we’re talking the 1920s or even the 1960s, there was a clear delineation back then between being “at home” and being “out,” and you dressed accordingly. Perhaps because we’re so accustomed to doing so many things at home that were once only done while out—working, shopping, watching movies, etc.—there seems to be less distinction between these two spheres today. Everyone simply dresses and acts as if they never left the couch.


We know anecdotally that public places feel less civil, a trend that seems to track with our increasing casualness. Don’t get me wrong—like others in the work-at-home economy, I spend most of my days in T-shirts. However, it’s a different matter when it comes to my old cars. Dressing the part to some degree, even if it’s merely donning a collared shirt, brings a sense of occasion to opening the garage. If you believe a calmer, more peaceful, more polite society is still possible, perhaps join me in leading with your wardrobe. I might be crazy, but if so, what’s the worst that can happen? Somebody will mistake you for having more class and taste than you do? Doesn’t sound so terrible.
